q: Is XGBoost a bagging or a boosting method?
raw:
__CUES__
1| Boosting
2| Sequential error correction

XGBoost is a boosting method, meaning it builds trees sequentially rather than in parallel. Each new tree is trained specifically to correct the residual errors made by the previous ones. This iterative optimization and built-in regularization are what make it exceptionally strong for tabular prediction tasks like the churn models I've built.

q: What's the time complexity of pushing onto a binary heap?
raw:
__CUES__
1| Logarithmic time complexity
2| Sift-up operation

Pushing onto a binary heap takes $O(\log n)$ time in the worst case. You add the new element to the next available position at the bottom of the tree to maintain the complete binary tree property, then sift it upward by swapping it with its parent until the heap invariant is restored.

q: What's the time complexity of pushing onto a binary heap?
raw:
__CUES__
1| O(log n) time complexity
2| Sift-up operation

Pushing onto a binary heap runs in $O(\log n)$ time. When you insert a new element at the next available leaf, you have to percolate or sift it up the tree by comparing it with its parent until the heap property is satisfied, which takes at most logarithmic time proportional to the height of the tree.

q: What's the time complexity of pushing onto a binary heap?
raw:
__CUES__
1| O(log n) complexity
2| Percolate up tree height

Pushing onto a binary heap takes $O(\log n)$ time. When you insert a new element, you place it at the next available leaf and bubble it upward by comparing it with its parent until the heap property is restored. Because a binary heap is a complete binary tree, its height is logarithmic relative to the number of items, so the worst-case number of operations is bounded by $\log n$.

q: What's the time complexity of pushing onto a binary heap?
raw:
__CUES__
1| O(log n) time complexity
2| Percolate up operation

Pushing onto a binary heap takes $O(\log n)$ time. You insert the new element at the bottom-most available spot—the end of the backing array—and then percolate it up by swapping it with its parent as long as it violates the heap property. Because the height of a complete binary tree with $n$ nodes is logarithmic, that upward path takes at most $\log n$ operations.

q: Why do Docker layers matter for build times?
raw:
__CUES__
1| Layer caching
2| Instruction ordering

Docker layers matter because the build engine caches each step as an immutable layer, reusing the cache if nothing changes. I structure my Dockerfiles to put slow-changing dependencies like package installs near the top and source code near the bottom. This prevents minor code edits from invalidating heavy caches and keeps build times fast.

q: Why do Docker layers matter for build times?
raw:
__CUES__
1| Layer caching and instruction order

Docker builds images as a stack of cached layers, reusing any step whose inputs haven't changed instead of rebuilding it from scratch. That's why instruction order is critical for fast builds. By placing items that rarely change, like system dependencies, before frequent code updates, we can skip heavy rebuild steps entirely on every push.

q: Why do Docker layers matter for build times?
raw:
__CUES__
1| Layer caching
2| Instruction ordering

Docker layers matter because the build engine caches each layer independently, meaning unmodified steps are skipped entirely on subsequent builds. By ordering our Dockerfile from least frequently changing instructions—like base images and dependency installations—to frequently changing source code, we maximize cache hits. This approach drastically cuts down CI/CD build times and speeds up our deployment pipelines.
